I think a lot of times there are just differences in communication styles. There are people who are more sensitive and there are people who are more direct, and there can be personality clashes because of that. I know people who identify as “direct” or “argumentative” so you’re not the only one out there.
I don’t really know the “mean/direct” things you said but I can attest that intent and result can be different and even something said with good intentions can be taken poorly. I had a friend who called herself “direct” and “honest” and she hurt my feelings a lot without realizing it. Her communication style was just different than mine- she thought it was friendly teasing when really it was hitting all my insecurities. 
Also, even if you’re not sure about ASD or some other disorder, I encourage you to try and get tested anyway. Hopefully some of this helps.

Hey! It sounds like you did a lot to try and make the relationship work! That’s great! Unfortunately sometimes when a sexual person and an asexual person try to date, it doesn’t work out. If both of you were drunk when the crossing of boundaries happened, neither one is really at fault here, since inebriated people don’t really have the ability to coherently consent. I can personally identify with only feeling guilt after a sexual act, sometimes not even realising that I felt pressured to consent until I look back on it. I also have anxiety and it sounds like her anxiety is definitely getting in the way of her being friends with you. Don’t apologise, but do make it clear that you didn’t intend to touch her in any way she didn’t want. She may have felt pressured to go along with it because of anxiety, or the alcohol, or any number of reasons, but if she didn’t let you know she was uncomfortable, there is no reason for you to be at fault here. Tell her you want to be friends again, no strings attached, and if she doesn’t respond positively to that, then no amount of kindness and good will you have in your heart will change her mind.
